tasks.title: The order of chains on a hook
tasks.statement: text is the output of nft list ruleset. Write a function hook_order(text, hook, version): return a list of strings 'family table chain' for the base chains attached to hook (input, forward, output, prerouting, postrouting) that see packets of IP version version (4 or 6), in the order the kernel runs them. A table of family ip applies to version 4, ip6 to version 6, inet to both; arp, bridge and netdev tables never apply. Skip regular chains (no 'type ... hook ...' line); lines inside set, map and flowtable blocks are neither rules nor chains. The line 'type T hook H [device D] priority P; policy X;' gives the priority P: an integer (maybe negative), the name raw -300, mangle -150, dstnat -100, filter 0, security 50, srcnat 100, or a name with an offset such as 'filter + 10' or 'srcnat - 5'. The smaller number runs first; with equal priorities keep the order of appearance in the text (the real order of equal priorities is not guaranteed).
tasks.hint: Parse the text line by line: table X Y {, chain Z {, the type ... line and set/map blocks; then sorted(..., key=priority) is stable and keeps the order of appearance.

tasks.title: The verdict for a packet
tasks.statement: text is the output of nft list ruleset, hook is the hook name, pkt is an IPv4 packet dictionary with the keys iif, proto (tcp, udp or icmp), saddr, daddr, sport, dport (None for icmp) and ct (new, established, related, invalid). Write a function packet_verdict(text, hook, pkt): return 'accept', 'drop' or 'reject'. Only base chains of type filter on hook hook in tables of families ip and inet count, in order of increasing priority (names as in nft: raw -300, mangle -150, dstnat -100, filter 0, security 50, srcnat 100, maybe with an offset such as 'filter + 10'; ties keep the order of appearance). Each chain gives a result: a drop or reject from it is final for the whole packet; accept ends only this chain and the packet goes on to the next one; if a chain ends without a verdict (or a return fires directly in the base chain, or after a goto), its policy applies (accept by default; accept means go on, drop is final). jump NAME enters a regular chain of the same table and, if it ended with no accept/drop/reject verdict, comes back to the next rule; return in a regular chain goes back; goto does not come back. If all chains are passed the answer is 'accept'. Set blocks (named sets with elements = { ... }, referred to as @name) and other blocks are not rules. A rule is a line of the listing. Conditions (all must hold, !=  negates the next value): ct state S, iif N or iifname N (the packet's iif), ip saddr A, ip daddr A, ip protocol P or meta l4proto P (the packet's proto), tcp dport V, udp dport V, tcp sport V, udp sport V (these also require the proto to be tcp or udp). A value is one item or a set in braces or a comma list; an item is a string (quotes are ignored), a port or a port range a-b, or an address, a CIDR network or an address range a-b. Statements to ignore: counter (also 'counter packets N bytes N'), log (also with prefix "..." and level L), comment "...". The first verdict word ends the rule: accept, drop, reject (also with extra words), return, jump NAME, goto NAME.
tasks.hint: Three layers: parse the listing, choose and sort the chains, walk the rules recursively for jump/goto. Decide chain by chain: an accept in a chain means 'go on'.

tasks.title: An nft script and the moment of lockout
tasks.statement: script is a script of nft commands, one per line (empty lines and lines starting with # are not commands; commands are numbered from 1). pkt is the dictionary of the administrator's already open session (as in the verdict task; ct is established). Write a function lockout(script, pkt): apply the commands in order to an empty ruleset and after each one check that the input hook lets the packet pkt through (verdict accept, computed as nft does: chains of type filter of tables ip and inet by priority, accept ends only its own chain, drop and reject are final, no verdict means the chain's policy). Return a tuple (the number of the first command after which the packet is dropped, or 0 if there was none; True if the packet is dropped after the last command). Commands: 'nft add table F T'; 'nft add chain F T C' (a regular chain) and 'nft add chain F T C { type filter hook H priority P \; [policy X \;] }' (a base chain, P is a number or a name filter/raw/mangle/dstnat/srcnat/security; without policy it is accept; the characters \; are written literally); 'nft add rule F T C TEXT' (to the end of the chain) and 'nft insert rule F T C TEXT' (to the beginning); 'nft flush chain F T C'; 'nft flush ruleset'; 'nft delete table F T'. A command that names a missing table or chain, or creates a chain that already exists, changes nothing (in nft it is an error). Chain rules are as simple as in the verdict task: the conditions ct state, iif/iifname, ip saddr/daddr, ip protocol, tcp/udp dport/sport and the verdicts accept, drop, reject (no jump or goto here). Values may be comma lists, ranges and CIDR networks.
tasks.hint: Keep the chains as dictionaries {fam, table, name, hook, prio, policy, rules}; recompute the verdict after every command. A regular chain without a hook does not influence the verdict.

tasks.title: Destination translation
tasks.statement: text is the output of nft list ruleset, pkt is a packet dictionary with the keys iif, proto (tcp or udp), daddr and dport, local_ip is the primary address of the incoming interface. Write a function nat_translate(text, pkt, local_ip): return the string 'address:port', where the first packet of a connection will be delivered after translation in the prerouting hook. Chains of type nat on the prerouting hook in tables ip and inet count, in order of increasing priority (names as in nft: dstnat -100, filter 0..., maybe with an offset such as 'dstnat + 5'; ties keep the order of appearance); chains of other types (filter) are ignored. Rules go in order; conditions stand before the word dnat or redirect (iifname N, ip daddr A, ip protocol P, tcp dport V, udp dport V; a value may be a set in braces, a range a-b or a CIDR network; != negates the value; counter statements, including 'counter packets N bytes N', are ignored). The first matching rule with dnat or redirect is executed and processing ends. 'dnat [ip] to A' changes the address, the port stays; 'dnat [ip] to A:P' changes the port too; 'dnat [ip] to tcp dport map { P1 : A1, P2 : A2 }' (or udp) takes the address by the destination port, the port stays, and the rule does not match if the packet's protocol differs or the port is not in the map (a failed lookup moves on to the next rule); 'redirect to P' and 'redirect to :P' replace the address with local_ip and the port with P. If nothing matched, return the original 'daddr:dport'.
tasks.hint: The conditions are everything before the word dnat/redirect: parse them the way you parse the conditions of ordinary rules. Remember that a map by port does not change the port.

tasks.title: Membership in a listed set
tasks.statement: text is the output of nft list set (or list ruleset with one set in it). Write a function set_contains(text, values): return a list of bool - whether each value from values belongs to the set. The type is given by the line 'type ipv4_addr', 'type ipv6_addr', 'type inet_service' or 'typeof ip saddr' / 'typeof ip daddr' (IPv4), 'typeof ip6 saddr' / 'typeof ip6 daddr' (IPv6), 'typeof tcp dport' / 'typeof udp dport' / 'typeof tcp sport' / 'typeof udp sport' (ports). For address sets values are address strings, for port sets they are integers. The elements are in the line(s) 'elements = { ... }', separated by commas, and may be wrapped onto following lines. An element is an address, a CIDR network or a range a-b (of addresses or ports); in a port set a service name may stand instead of a number: ssh 22, domain 53, http 80, https 443, smtp 25, imap 143, mysql 3306. After an element the words timeout T, expires T and comment "..." may follow - they do not change the element itself. If there is no elements line the set is empty.
tasks.hint: re.search(r'elements = \{(.*?)\}', text, re.S); each element is the first word after splitting on commas. Convert everything to integers and compare with ranges.

tasks.title: Connection tracking and input
tasks.statement: Write a function ct_replay(policy, rules, events): policy is 'accept' or 'drop' (the policy of the input chain), rules is a list of rule strings of this chain, events is a list of tuples (direction, proto, src, sport, dst, dport) in order of arrival; direction 'out' is a packet created by the host itself (the output chain accepts everything but the connection is tracked), 'in' is a packet that arrived on interface eth0 and goes to the input chain. Return a list of verdicts ('accept', 'drop' or 'reject') for each event; for 'out' always 'accept'. The ct state of a packet is computed like this: if the connection table has no entry with the tuple (proto, src, sport, dst, dport) nor with the reverse (proto, dst, dport, src, sport), the state is new; a packet matching an entry's forward tuple is new until a reply has been accepted and established afterwards; a packet matching the reverse tuple is established. An entry is created only if its first packet is accepted; 'reply seen' is recorded only when a reply packet is accepted; dropped packets create or change nothing. rules use the conditions ct state, iif/iifname (packets arrive on eth0), ip saddr, ip daddr, ip protocol, tcp/udp dport/sport and the verdicts accept, drop, reject; the first verdict decides, otherwise the policy applies. Values are as in nft: comma lists, sets, ranges a-b, CIDR networks.
tasks.hint: Keep a dictionary of forward tuples -> {'replied': bool}. Compute the state first, then the verdict, and change the table only after an accept.

tasks.title: firewall-cmd --list-all to permissions
tasks.statement: text is the output of firewall-cmd --list-all (the layout of firewalld 2.x: the first line is the zone name and optional marks in parentheses separated by commas, such as 'public (default, active)'; then lines '  key: values' with two spaces; for forward-ports and rich rules the values are on the following lines that start with a tab; an empty value may have no space after the colon; ignore other keys). services is a dictionary of services {name: list of 'port/protocol' strings}. Write a function firewall_summary(text, services): return a dictionary with the keys zone (the name), default and active (bool, from the marks), target ('reject' for default and %%REJECT%%, 'accept' for ACCEPT, 'drop' for DROP), open (a sorted list of unique 'port/protocol' strings from the zone's services (skip unknown services) and from ports; ranges such as 9000-9010/tcp are kept; sort by protocol as a string, then by first port, then by last port), protocols (a sorted list from protocols), masquerade (bool), rich (a list of strings from rich rules in output order) and forwards (a list from forward-ports). A rich rule gives strings 'action target from source', where the action is the last word of the rule (accept, reject or drop; skip rules whose last word is anything else), the source is source address="..." or 'any', the target is 'port/protocol' for port port="P" protocol="T", one string per port of the service for service name="S" (in the service's list order), or 'all' if the rule has neither a port nor a service; skip rules with masquerade, forward-port, icmp-block, icmp-type, protocol and source-port. A forward-ports line 'port=P:proto=T:toport=Q:toaddr=A' gives 'P/T -> A:Q' (an empty toport means the same port P, an empty toaddr stays empty).
tasks.hint: Lines without leading whitespace are the header, tab lines continue the previous key. Sort ports with the key (protocol, start, end).

tasks.title: Choosing a firewalld zone
tasks.statement: active is the output of firewall-cmd --get-active-zones: a line with the zone name (the name may be followed by ' (default)'), below it the lines '  interfaces: ...' and '  sources: ...' with values separated by spaces; sources may hold CIDR networks (IPv4 and IPv6), MAC addresses and ipset:name. priorities is a dictionary {zone: ingress-priority}, zones outside it have priority 0. Write a function zone_select(active, priorities, default_zone, iface, saddr): return the name of the zone that will handle a packet that arrived on interface iface from address saddr. A candidate zone is a zone whose sources contain a network that holds saddr (ignore MAC addresses and ipsets) or whose interfaces contain iface; if both hold, the zone counts as a source candidate. The candidate with the smaller priority wins; with equal priorities source candidates come before interface candidates, and inside a group by zone name in alphabetical order. If there are no candidates, return default_zone.
tasks.hint: The sort key of a candidate: (priority, 0 if by source else 1, name). ipaddress.ip_network(s, strict=False) raises ValueError on a MAC and an ipset.

tasks.title: Unreachable rules
tasks.statement: rules is a list of rule strings of one chain in order, as in an nft listing. Write a function shadowed_rules(rules): return a list of tuples (i, j), numbers from 1: rule i can never fire because an earlier rule j catches the packet first (take the very first such j) and the packet gets j's verdict. Rule j catches rule i when it is terminal and everything it checks is wider than or equal to what i checks. A terminal rule is a rule where, after the conditions and the statements counter (including 'counter packets N bytes N'), log (including with prefix "..." and level L) and comment "...", there is accept, drop or reject, followed by nothing or only comment "..."; jump, goto, return and any other statements (such as limit) make a rule unknown: it catches nothing and is not itself checked (it never appears in the answer). A rule with != or an unknown condition is unknown too. The conditions of a rule: ct state (a set), iif/iifname (a set of strings), ip saddr and ip daddr (CIDR networks, addresses or a list in braces), ip protocol P and meta l4proto P (protocol), tcp dport and udp dport (a set of ports, including ranges a-b; they also set protocol tcp/udp), icmp type T (protocol icmp and a set of types). The condition of rule j is wider than or equal to that of rule i if for every field in j's condition: the field is also in i and i's set is inside j's set (for addresses each network of i lies inside one network of j; for protocol the values are equal). A field that j does not have restricts nothing.
tasks.hint: Turn each rule into a dictionary field->set (expand ports into set(range)). For a pair (j, i) check inclusion for every field of j.

tasks.title: iptables-save to open ports
tasks.statement: text is the output of iptables-save. Write a function iptables_open_ports(text, src, iface): only the table *filter and the chain INPUT count; return a dictionary {'policy': the INPUT policy in lowercase ('accept' if there is no :INPUT line), 'tcp': a sorted list of ports, 'udp': the same}. A port goes into the list of a protocol if any rule mentions it as --dport P, --dport A:B (a range including A and B) or --dports P1,P2,A:B (multiport), and a NEW connection from address src through interface iface would get ACCEPT in the INPUT chain for it. Rules are walked in order; every condition of a rule must hold: -s network (an address or CIDR), -i interface, -p tcp|udp|icmp|all, --dport, --dports, -m conntrack --ctstate L and -m state --state L (a comma list; it holds if NEW is in it), and conditions with ! before -s or -i are negated. The modules -m tcp, -m udp, -m multiport, -m comment (with --comment "...") and -m state/-m conntrack only introduce their options. The target after -j: ACCEPT, DROP, REJECT (with any options) end the check, LOG does not (go on to the next rule), RETURN leaves a user chain back, any other name is a user chain (entered like a jump; if the chain ended with no verdict, continue after the jump). If INPUT ended with no verdict, the policy applies (ACCEPT or DROP).
tasks.hint: Collect rules per chain (-A NAME), policies from ':NAME POLICY' lines, candidate ports from all --dport/--dports; for each (protocol, port) walk INPUT recursively.
